cim: Israel Plans National AI Model to Reduce Foreign Dependence, Protect Control of Critical Infrastructure
cim_eredeti: Israel Plans National AI Model to Reduce Foreign Dependence, Protect Control of Critical Infrastructure
szoveg_eredeti:
Israel plans to develop its own artificial intelligence model to reduce dependence on foreign technology and maintain control over critical national infrastructure as AI becomes increasingly central to government operations, the head of its National AI Directorate announced Monday.

Brig. Gen. (res.) Erez Askal, head of the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister’s Office, outlined the initiative during his opening address at AI Week at Tel Aviv University on November 9, 2026.

The proposed infrastructure includes 2 gigawatts of energy capacity, 100,000 graphics processing units (GPUs), an Israeli quantum computer and a nationally controlled foundation AI model. Askal also called for substantial investment in workforce training and technological development.

He warned that growing dependence on artificial intelligence would fundamentally change the relationship between technology and national sovereignty.

“We are on the threshold of a new reality of sovereignty. Within a few years, national infrastructure will operate on the basis of artificial intelligence. Whoever controls it will control the switch that powers nations.”

Alongside the infrastructure plans, Israel launched the National Institute for Impact-Driven Artificial Intelligence, operating under the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister’s Office.

The institute will coordinate government ministries, businesses, universities, civil society organizations and philanthropic institutions to develop practical AI applications addressing public needs.

Its activities will cover nine national challenges, including health care, population aging, education, national resilience, environmental and climate issues, equality and economic growth.

Under its initial operating plan, the institute will undertake 10 to 14 initiatives annually, aiming to advance five of its first 10 projects into implementation within one year.

Askal also presented a broader five-year framework for addressing 10 challenges annually by identifying regulatory, technological, procedural or data-related obstacles.

Potential applications include improving fourth-grade mathematics education, reducing congestion on Highway 6 and improving initial doctor-patient consultations.

Rather than limiting projects to technological development or pilot programs, the institute intends to measure improvements in everyday services and transfer successful applications to organizations capable of maintaining them independently.

Askal additionally emphasized the need for flexible regulation, cybersecurity protections, ethical oversight and clear accountability for AI systems and their outcomes.
